name: Rebecca Purple
lede: Rebecca Purple is a deep, saturated purple added to the CSS color keywords in 2014 in memory of Rebecca Alison Meyer, who died of brain cancer on her sixth birthday, at her own request named for her full name rather than the nickname "Becca."

sections.title: A memorial written into a web standard
sections.body: Rebecca Alison Meyer, the daughter of web-standards writer Eric Meyer, died of a brain tumor in June 2014, twelve hours into her sixth birthday [1]. Purple was her favorite color [1]. After the news spread, designer and author Jeffrey Zeldman started a campaign to have the hex value #663399 added to CSS under the name "beccapurple" in her memory [2]. Eric Meyer asked for one change: call it rebeccapurple instead [1][2]. He explained that Rebecca had insisted, once she turned six, on being called by her full name rather than the childhood nickname Becca, which she considered a baby name [1]. The CSS Working Group approved the addition that same month, and it shipped as part of the CSS Color Module Level 4 — one of a very small number of named colors in the official CSS specification tied to a real person rather than a pigment, a place, or a trade name [2][3].

sections.title: Its neighbors
sections.body: In the color graph, Rebecca Purple sits 3.2 units from [[wood-violet]], duller, and 3.8 units from [[spectrum-violet]], almost the same color [4]. [[campanula]] and [[ksu-purple]], both 4.8 units off, are duller and darker respectively; [[seance]], 4.9 off, is darker; the basic term [[purple]], 5.1 off, is lighter [4]. None of the six is close enough to be the same color [4]: Rebecca Purple sits in its own small, distinctly saturated patch of violet-purple.

sections.title: Seen in
sections.body: Its two nearest gem twins are Amethyst, 3.4 units off, and Tanzanite, 6.3 off [5]. On screen, Wes Anderson's *The Grand Budapest Hotel*, built around a distinctive violet-purple uniform and hotel livery, lands 3.8 units away, and Kurosawa's *Dreams* sits 5.1 off [6]. A fashion-history marker for the nineteenth-century aniline-dye craze, keyed to Hofmann's violet, one of the first wave of synthetic purple dyes, sits 3.1 units off — an odd, unplanned echo between the first synthetic purple and the most recent named one [7]. Among design aesthetics, 1960s psychedelia and Neon noir both land 2.3 units off on this color's neighbor Seance, with Pastel Goth a step further at 3.3 units on Rebecca Purple itself [8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our 23,778-painting archive carries this color covering even 1 percent of its canvas, as photographed [9]. That is an expected result, not a gap: this is a 2014 CSS color keyword, newer than almost every painting old enough to be in a museum archive, so there was never a historical chance for it to appear [9]. This is a computed color match on photographed, varnished canvases, not a pigment test — the honest field note here is simply that the method and the color's own age do not overlap.

questions.q: Why did Eric Meyer ask for the color to be called "rebeccapurple" rather than the originally proposed "beccapurple"?
choices: Rebecca wanted to be called by her full name, not the nickname Becca, once she turned six
Becca was already taken as a CSS color name
Rebeccapurple tested better with focus groups
It was a typo that became permanent
questions.answer: Rebecca wanted to be called by her full name, not the nickname Becca, once she turned six

choices: It is a 2014 color, newer than nearly every painting in a museum archive
Purple pigments do not photograph accurately
The archive excludes purple colors entirely
Rebecca Purple is too similar to black to register
questions.answer: It is a 2014 color, newer than nearly every painting in a museum archive

openers: One of the handful of named colors in the official CSS specification exists because of a six-year-old's own request about her name.
The first wave of synthetic purple dye and the most recent named purple in CSS sit only 3.1 units apart, by coincidence alone.

issues: Depth wave pilot: no book concordance exists for this modern CSS color, so the story is sourced from the web (Eric Meyer's own primary-source blog post, plus a secondary account), hedged and both given real urls. The color graph, archive fieldnotes (an honest zero) and gem/film/look twins supply the rest.
